findings.title: Async legacy writes inherit the request cancellation context
findings.body: The goroutine derives its 10-second context from the original request context. HTTP/API-server request contexts are normally canceled as soon as the handler returns, which happens immediately after this goroutine is started, so the legacy Create will usually receive an already-canceled context rather than up to 10 seconds to complete. The same pattern is used by Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection (lines 110, 135, and 163), making the asynchronous replication unreliable or effectively skipped for normal completed requests. Detach cancellation (while preserving required context values/logging) before applying the timeout.

findings.title: Independent replication goroutines can apply mutations out of order
findings.body: Each successful write starts an independent goroutine with no per-resource ordering or serialization. For example, a successful unified Create followed immediately by Delete can run the legacy Delete first and the legacy Create second, leaving an object in legacy that no longer exists in unified storage. Consecutive updates can similarly overwrite newer legacy state with an older update. Since legacy APIs remain available as the stated safety measure, this produces persistent cross-store divergence; replication needs an ordered queue/keyed serialization or another ordering mechanism.

findings.title: Legacy Update re-executes the original UpdatedObjectInfo instead of replaying the unified result
findings.body: After Storage.Update has already evaluated objInfo against the unified object, the asynchronous legacy update receives the original objInfo and evaluates it again against legacy state. This regresses the prior implementation, which evaluated the update once and wrapped the resulting object for each store. UpdatedObjectInfo can represent a PATCH/apply operation and can depend on the old object, resource version, managed fields, or request-specific state; evaluating it again can yield a different object or fail due to the legacy object's version. As a result, successful unified updates may not be mirrored correctly to legacy. Capture and replay the object produced by the unified update (using an appropriate wrapper) rather than reusing objInfo.

findings.title: Delete metrics use object names as the kind label
findings.body: The successful Delete metric passes `name` where the metric helper's kind/resource label is expected, unlike the error path and all other methods which pass `options.Kind`. Every distinct object name will create a separate Prometheus time series, causing unbounded metric cardinality on deletes and making the kind dimension incorrect. Pass `options.Kind` here.

findings.title: Legacy DeleteCollection duration is recorded as a storage duration
findings.body: The asynchronous legacy DeleteCollection call records its result through `recordStorageDuration`, so storage metrics are double-counted and no legacy duration/error metric is emitted for this operation. This makes monitoring of replication failures and latency inaccurate; call `recordLegacyDuration` instead.

findings.title: Create storage failures are attributed to legacy metrics
findings.body: When Storage.Create fails, the code calls `recordLegacyDuration` rather than `recordStorageDuration`. The analogous Update error path at line 129 has the same issue. Storage write failures in mode 3 will therefore be missing from storage error metrics and falsely inflate legacy errors, obscuring which backend failed.

findings.title: Mode 3 tests do not verify asynchronous legacy replication
findings.body: The tests return immediately after the unified operation and never wait for or assert the background legacy call. Moreover, both `legacyStoreMock` and `storageMock` share one testify Mock and define identical method expectations, so an expectation configured as a storage call can also satisfy the legacy call; there is no `AssertExpectations` call to establish that either occurred. Consequently these tests would pass if replication never runs (including when the caller context is canceled), and they do not detect the ordering or Update replay regressions. Use distinct backend mocks and synchronization (for example a channel/WaitGroup) to assert the legacy call and its arguments.
